newsitem.title: ALBANIA: 17 killed as Berisha prepares to meet EU mission.
newsitem.headline: 17 killed as Berisha prepares to meet EU mission.

text.p: Seventeen people died in a shoot-out in central Albania, the worst bloodletting in two months of unrest in the Balkan state as it seeks foreign help to pull it from the brink of anarchy.
State news agency ATA said the killings began when a group of 16 armed people murdered a local leader in the village of Levan in central Albania on Thursday evening.

"Local people, now armed as many other people in Albania...surrounded the group and killed them all. This is the event with the heaviest toll during the past two months in Albania," ATA said. No independent confirmation was available.

President Sali Berisha is to meet European relief experts in Tirana on Friday to discuss the country's aid needs and deployment of a multinational force to protect humanitarian shipments to the former communist state.
Much of southern Albania is ruled by armed gangs who blame Berisha for the collapse of popular savings schemes in January in which thousands of people lost everything.
ATA said the 16 gunmen were killed by local people indignant at the killing of the chairman of the council of elders of Levan.
It gave no motive for the shooting of the chairman and did not name any of the dead nor say whether they belonged to rival political groups.

The killings added to a death toll of already well over 100 in the insurrection and banditry. Most military depots have been looted and prisoners released. Most foreign nationals were evacuated this month.
Berisha is due to meet a delegation headed by Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg on Friday morning for talks on a posssible protection force as well as plans for early elections in June.

Europe's top security body, the OSCE, on Thursday welcomed an initiative for an international protection force in Albania but said it was up to the United Nations Security Council to approve the mission.
Six European Union countries -- Italy, France, Spain, Portugal, Greece and Austria -- have military experts in Albania to prepare for the security force. Turkey and Romania have also offered to help.
D'Ansembourg has said any force could range up to about 3,000 personnel -- police, gendarmes or military police.
He also said he "was especially going to discuss the election issue with Mr Berisha". Berisha signed a pact with a new unity government on March 9 calling for elections by June.
D'Ansembourg said Justice Minister Spartak Ngjela had suggested a slight delay, telling him that "June might be too early while August would be too late."
Also on Friday, the International Committee of the Red Cross is to renew efforts to transport aid overland into southern Albania in a test of perilous roads held by bandits.
Two Red Cross vehicles returned into Greece after waiting in vain for several hours at a southern border post on Thursday for word from relief workers that it was safe to cross.

New local authorities in the southern town of Vlore have invited mayors and rebel councils to meet on Friday for talks on how to resolve the crisis. They are likely to renew calls for Berisha's resignation.
On Thursday, the Albanian parliament approved a bill granting amnesty for up to 800 of about 1,300 prisoners in Albania's jails who escaped in lawlessness this month.
The amnesty law also offer incentives to more serious offenders, hoping to lure them back to their cells.
It cuts life sentences to 20 years and offers a third off sentences for convicts returning by April 5.
